summary.text: Velocity measures both how fast an object moves and the specific direction of its motion.
An object undergoes acceleration whenever there is a change in its speed, its direction, or both.
Average velocity over a period of time is the change in position divided by the duration of that period, written v̄ = Δs/Δt.

items.prompt: A race car travels around a circular track at a steady speed of 100 kilometers per hour. Why is the car considered to be accelerating?

options.label: Its average speed is lower than its instantaneous speed.
Its direction of motion changes continuously as it turns.
Its total displacement is increasing at a non-linear rate.
Its speed is constantly increasing to maintain the curve.

items.explain: Acceleration occurs whenever speed, direction, or both change. Because moving in a circle changes the car's direction continuously, it is accelerating despite its steady speed.

items.prompt: A runner completes one full 400-meter circular lap and finishes right back at the start line. How does their average velocity compare to their average speed?

options.label: Average velocity is less than average speed because total displacement is zero.
Average velocity is greater than average speed because direction was changing.
Average velocity and average speed are equal because motion took place.
Average velocity cannot be calculated without knowing the instantaneous acceleration.

items.explain: While distance continuously accumulates, displacement can return to zero. Because displacement is zero over the full lap, average velocity is less than the average speed.

items.prompt: A space probe launches at 11,200 meters per second to leave Earth. Why is calling this threshold 'escape velocity' technically inaccurate?

options.label: The object escapes only if it moves in a counter-clockwise direction.
The value changes depending on which reference frame is chosen.
Escaping depends only on reaching that speed, regardless of direction.
The measurement refers strictly to angular speed around the planet.

items.explain: Any object reaching that speed magnitude will escape Earth regardless of the direction it travels, making 'escape speed' the more precise scientific term.

items.prompt: If you look at a graph with position on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis, how do you determine the instantaneous velocity at one precise moment?

options.label: Calculate the total area underneath the position curve.
Multiply the position coordinate by the time coordinate.
Find the slope of the line tangent to the curve at that point.
Find the slope of the secant line between the start and end times.

items.explain: On a position-time graph, instantaneous velocity is represented by the slope of the line tangent to the curve at that exact point.

items.prompt: Car A and car B are both driving on a highway, each with its own velocity vector. How do you find A’s velocity as measured from B?

options.label: Add B’s velocity vector to A’s velocity vector
Divide A’s speed by B’s speed along the road
Average the two velocity vectors together
Subtract B’s velocity vector from A’s velocity vector

items.explain: The velocity of A relative to B is defined as the difference of the two velocity vectors, v − w.

items.prompt: How does relative velocity behave in classical Newtonian mechanics compared to special relativity?

options.label: It is independent of reference frames in Newtonian mechanics but frame-dependent in relativity.
It depends on the reference frame in Newtonian mechanics but is frame-independent in relativity.
It can only be calculated in special relativity when using polar coordinates.
It is identical to scalar speed in Newtonian mechanics but equals acceleration in relativity.

items.explain: In Newtonian mechanics, the calculated relative velocity remains the same regardless of the chosen inertial reference frame, whereas in special relativity it varies based on the frame.
